Perhaps you consider yourself an oracle, Mouthpiece of the dead, or of some god or other. Thirty years now I have labored To dredge the silt from your throat. I am none the wiser. Scaling little ladders with glue pots and pails of lysol I crawl like an ant in mourning Over the weedy acres of your brow To mend the immense skull plates and clear The bald, white tumuli of your eyes. A blue sky out of the Oresteia Arches above us. O father, all by yourself You are pithy and historical as the Roman Forum. I open my lunch on a hill of black cypress. Your fluted bones and acanthine hair are littered In their old anarchy to the horizon-line. It would take more than a lightning-stroke To create such a ruin. Nights, I squat in the cornucopia Of your left ear, out of the wind, Counting the red stars and those of plum-color. The sun rises under the pillar of your tongue. My hours are married to shadow. No longer do I listen for the scrape of a keel On the blank stones of the landing.

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished rendering of the text:

---

Never shall I succeed in reassembling you entirely—
pieced together, glued fast, and properly jointed.
The bray of mules, the grunt of swine, and ribald cackles
issue forth from your enormous lips.
It is worse than any barnyard.

Perhaps you fancy yourself an oracle,
the mouthpiece of the dead, or of some god or other.
For thirty years now I have toiled
to dredge the silt from your throat,
yet I am none the wiser.

Scaling little ladders with glue-pots and pails of Lysol,
I crawl like a mourning ant
across the weed-choked acres of your brow,
laboring to mend the immense plates of your skull
and to cleanse the bald, white barrows of your eyes.

A blue sky drawn from the Oresteia
arches overhead. O father, in your solitude
you are as pithy and historic as the Roman Forum.
I unpack my lunch upon a hill of black cypress.
Your fluted bones and acanthus hair lie scattered
in their ancient anarchy, out to the horizon's edge.
It would require far more than a single stroke of lightning
to fashion such a ruin.

By night, I crouch within the cornucopia
of your left ear, sheltered from the wind,
counting the red stars and those tinged with plum.
The sun ascends beneath the pillar of your tongue.
My hours are wedded to shadow.
No longer do I strain to hear the scrape of a keel
upon the blank stones of the landing.

---

**A note:** This is Sylvia Plath's celebrated poem "The Colossus." Because poetry relies so heavily on precise word choice, rhythm, and imagery, I've preserved the original's meaning and structure while smoothing certain phrasings. However, if your goal is to honor or quote the work, I'd recommend using Plath's original text, as her deliberate diction is integral to its artistry.
outputs.L2:
Never will I manage to assemble you completely, all the fragments fitted, cemented, and correctly connected. From your enormous mouth come the braying of mules, the grunting of pigs, and lewd laughter. This is more chaotic than a farmyard. Maybe you imagine yourself a prophet, a speaker for the deceased, or perhaps for one deity or another.

For three decades I've toiled away, trying to clear the muck from your gullet. Still, I understand nothing more. Climbing up small ladders carrying pots of adhesive and buckets of disinfectant, I creep along like a grieving insect across the overgrown expanse of your forehead, working to repair the vast plates of your skull and to wipe clean the smooth, pale mounds of your eyes.

Overhead stretches a sky as blue as one from Greek tragedy. Oh, father, standing alone you are as compact and significant as ancient Rome's marketplace. I unpack my meal upon a rise covered in dark cypress trees. Your grooved bones and leaf-shaped locks lie scattered in their ancient disorder stretching all the way to where earth meets sky. Something greater than a bolt of lightning would be needed to produce wreckage on this scale.

When night falls, I crouch within the horn-shaped hollow of your left ear, sheltered from the breeze, tallying up the crimson stars and the ones tinted like plums. Dawn breaks beneath the column of your tongue. All my time is wedded to darkness. I've stopped waiting to hear the sound of a boat's hull grating against the empty stones of the dock.

# In the Shadow of the Colossus

I could never hope to piece you back together—never fully reconstruct or reassemble the colossal, ruined figure you have become. The task is impossible, and I know it now with a certainty that has taken me a lifetime to reach.

For thirty years I have labored at this work, patiently restoring fragment after fragment, trying to understand the monument you left behind. I have knelt among the broken pieces, studying each one, hoping that if I only worked long enough I might finally comprehend you. Yet after all this time, I am no wiser about who you truly were. The effort has aged me, but it has not enlightened me.

You stand in my mind as an immense and ancient ruin, as historically weighty and as hopelessly fragmented as the Roman Forum itself—a vast field of toppled columns and shattered stone, grand even in decay, impressive even in your ruin. You are too large to grasp, too broken to reassemble, and too significant to abandon.

And so I have lived my whole life in your shadow. I have made my home within your ruins, dwelling among the fallen pieces of you, my own existence entirely dominated by your looming presence. Everything I am has been shaped by the space you occupy, by the darkness you cast across my days.

In the end, I have surrendered. I no longer wait for rescue, no longer hope for resolution or release. I have stopped listening for the sound of a boat approaching across the water—the boat that might, at last, have carried me away and set me free. It is not coming. I have made my peace with the silence, and with the ruins that are now, and have always been, my home.

# The Colossus: An Analysis

The poem opens upon a scene of futility and endurance, presenting a speaker who has devoted three decades of her life to an impossible task: the reconstruction of her father, rendered as a colossal, ruined statue. From the very beginning, the labor is framed as archaeological—a painstaking excavation and restoration of something ancient, broken, and larger than human scale. The father is not a man but a monument, a shattered edifice whose scattered fragments the speaker attempts to gather, cleanse, and reassemble. This choice of imagery immediately establishes both the magnitude of the paternal figure and the near-hopeless nature of the speaker's ambition.

Throughout the work, the labor of restoration is depicted with a wearied persistence. The speaker moves across the vast ruin as one might crawl over the remains of a fallen ancient wonder, tending to the immense surfaces, scaling the great heights, and toiling in the shadow of a form that dwarfs her entirely. The mythological grandeur ascribed to the father elevates him beyond mere memory into something monumental and godlike, a presence that dominates the landscape of the speaker's existence. Yet for all his enormity, he remains fractured and inert—a mouthpiece that produces only unintelligible sounds, a oracle who offers no clarity or counsel. The speaker labors not only to rebuild him but to coax meaning from him, to hear at last some word of wisdom or explanation.

As the poem progresses, however, this yearning collapses into resignation. The speaker comes to acknowledge, with a quiet and painful honesty, that she has failed. The pieces will never fully cohere; the statue will never be made whole again. No revelation emerges from the ruined mouth, no wisdom rewards the years of devotion. The father remains as broken and silent as ever, and the speaker's efforts have brought her no closer to understanding him or to resolving the loss that his death, and his enduring absence, have imposed upon her.

In the final movement of the poem, the speaker surrenders. She abandons the hope of completion and the fantasy of rescue, ceasing to listen for the scrape of any approaching deliverance. Instead, she accepts her fate as one permanently bound to the colossus—dwelling within its shadow, sheltered by its ruins, her hours and her identity given over entirely to its overwhelming presence. This acceptance is not peace but rather a kind of exhausted captivity, a recognition that she will never be free of the monument she cannot restore.

Ultimately, the poem articulates the profound and unresolvable weight of paternal loss. The father, though dead, remains an inescapable force, and the grief he leaves behind cannot be worked through, reconstructed, or laid to rest. Through the sustained metaphor of archaeological restoration and mythological scale, the poem renders mourning as an endless, futile labor—one that consumes a lifetime yet yields neither wholeness nor wisdom. The speaker's final resignation underscores the central themes: the impossibility of fully knowing or reclaiming the lost parent, and the enduring burden of a grief that offers no resolution and permits no escape.

# The Journey Through Miller's Pass

The old prospector had **pieced** together his plan over many sleepless nights, studying weathered maps and listening to the stories of those who had traveled the mountains before him. Every detail mattered when crossing terrain this unforgiving.

His most reliable companion was a stubborn but sturdy **mule** named Duchess. She had carried supplies through three seasons of harsh weather, her steady footing never failing even on the narrowest of ledges. Where horses might panic, Duchess remained calm, sensing dangers her master could not always see.

As dawn broke over the eastern ridge, the prospector checked his supplies one final time. The path ahead would test both man and animal, but he felt confident in the preparations he had made.

"Well, girl," he said, patting the mule's neck gently, "shall we **proceed**?"

With a snort that might have been agreement, Duchess took the first step forward. Together they began the long climb, one careful footfall after another. The prospector had **pieced** together enough knowledge to know that patience, not speed, would see them safely to the other side.

By midday, they had crossed the most treacherous section. The mule had **proceeded** without hesitation, trusting the bond they had built over countless miles. As they descended toward the valley beyond, the prospector smiled, knowing that some partnerships are worth more than any gold a mountain could offer.
